title: Tool comparison guide: PMS, dynamic pricing, AI guest messaging

slides.title: Your weights and a real trial pick the stack, not a best-tool list
slides.subtitle: Resource SR.5. Tool comparison guide: PMS, dynamic pricing, AI guest messaging
meta: Alder Street unit and Cedar Ridge house (hypothetical)
Education only. Not legal, tax, or software-purchase advice.
slides.notes:
This resource is a worksheet for choosing your software. It covers three jobs: the property management system or channel manager, dynamic pricing, and AI guest messaging. Your stack is the set of tools you run together.

You'll notice it never names a best tool. The right stack for one apartment on two channels is often wrong for a lake house that plans a direct-booking site next year. So the sheet has you describe your operation, weight what matters to it, run a real trial, and score what you saw.

I'll walk through each part of the template. Then we'll run the same two hypothetical tools, Tool X and Tool Y, against Alder Street and Cedar Ridge. The same two tools give different answers for each, because the weights are different. That's the whole lesson in one example.

Nothing here is a vendor recommendation. Every price on the sheet stays blank until you fill it from the vendor's own page.

Sam and I split this cleanly. Sam records the course's live software demos, and his lessons carry codes like 9.12 and OP.4. Sam's 9.12 and 9.13 show how Guesty and PriceLabs work, screen by screen. His OP.4 and OP.5 show owners how to wire the pieces into one workflow. I'm not going to repeat any of that.

This sheet is where you compare candidates, test the handoffs between them, and write down the decision. When I mention Guesty or PriceLabs, it's only as an example of a category those lessons cover.

When you watch Sam's demos, bring back three things from each one. First, which Airbnb sync mode he chooses. Second, where rates get edited. Third, how you'd review a change the software made on its own. Those three answers feed straight into this sheet.

Owners, the same applies to OP.4 and OP.5. Watch them with the operator profile open.

slides.title: Four pieces pass data through the PMS, and the failures sit at the handoffs

nodes.d: Holds listing, calendar, rates. Pushes to Airbnb, Vrbo, direct
Sends rates and minimum stays back to the PMS, or straight to a channel
Reads reservations from the PMS; sends guest messages
Handled by whoever is merchant of record on each channel

box.label: Test the handoffs
box.text: A rate set in two places. A block that reaches Airbnb but not Vrbo. A message with an old door code. A tax nobody remits on direct bookings.

slides.notes:
Before you score anything, draw the flow for your own operation. Most small stacks look like this.

The PMS or channel manager holds the listing, the calendar, and the rates. It pushes them out to Airbnb, Vrbo, and a direct site if you have one. Reservations flow back into it. The pricing tool sends rates and minimum stays back to the PMS, or straight to a channel. The messaging layer reads reservations from the PMS and sends guest messages. Payment and tax are handled by whoever is the merchant of record on each channel.

So every arrow here is really a handoff to or from the PMS. The screens usually work. The problems show up at those handoffs. A rate set in two places. A calendar block that reaches one channel and not the other. A message quoting last month's door code. So your trial should test the handoffs, not just the screens.

slides.title: Connecting a PMS can move where you edit, who takes payment, and who remits tax

left.head: Airbnb: two sync choices
items: [Sync everything](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2348): edit details, photos, pricing, and availability only in your software. Those fields gray out on Airbnb
Sync pricing and availability only: content and booking settings stay on Airbnb

right.head: Vrbo: once integrated
items: Per the [integration article](https://help.vrbo.com/articles/About-Vrbo-integration), no edits to availability, bookings, or rates in the Owner Dashboard
Rates and availability update within a few hours; content in 24 to 48 hours
You may become [merchant of record](https://help.vrbo.com/articles/IPM-About-payments-for-integrated-accounts), handling payments, tax collection, and remittance

slides.notes:
Two platform rules shape the flow. First, one term. The merchant of record is the business that charges the guest's card and answers for that payment, including refunds and, often, the tax.

Airbnb gives connected hosts two sync choices. With sync everything, you edit listing details, photos, pricing, and availability only through your software. Those fields gray out on Airbnb. With sync pricing and availability only, content and booking settings stay on Airbnb.

Vrbo says that once a listing is integrated, you can't edit availability, bookings, or rates in the Owner Dashboard. Rates and availability update within a few hours; content takes 24 to 48 hours.

Here's the big one. Vrbo says that depending on your setup, you may become the merchant of record, handling payments and lodging tax. Ask your vendor in writing whether your setup does that. These pages cover Vrbo only, so ask about Airbnb too.

So connecting a PMS can move where you edit, who takes the money, and who handles lodging tax.

box.label: Merchant of record
box.text: **Merchant of record:** the business that charges the guest's card and is responsible for that payment, including refunds and, often, the tax.

slides.title: Fill the operator profile first, including who takes payment and remits tax
rows: Must it appear in every listing?
Where a rating below 3 disqualifies a tool
slides.notes:
The operator profile comes before any trial. It's a description of your business, not of the software. In the Status column, write done, or confirm with and a name.

Start with property count now and in a year, your channels, and whether you need direct booking and when. Then your team: who answers messages, who schedules cleaners, who handles repairs. Then the software budget, taken from your underwriting model.

The middle rows connect to SR.1. For each channel, who is the merchant of record and who remits each lodging tax? Does the city require the permit number in every listing? You already found those answers in SR.1 Sections C and D. Copy them here, because the software has to support them.

Then your lock or access system, and whether it makes a new code for each stay.

The last row matters most. Must-haves are the criteria where a rating below 3 knocks a tool out, whatever its total. Decide them now, before you've seen any tool.

slides.caption: Rate each criterion 1 to 5 (SR.5.6). Save the evidence: screenshots, vendor emails, logs, and the reconciled sheet.
slides.notes:
For the PMS, every criterion has a test you actually run. A vendor's feature list tells you what they claim. The trial tells you what happens on your listing.

A few of these are worth slowing down on. Single source of truth: change a rate in the PMS, then try to change it on Airbnb, and see which one wins. You want one place to edit, with overrides blocked or flagged.

Permissions: make a login for your cleaner and check that it can't see payouts. Owner statements: export the trial period and reconcile at least a week of it to what the channels actually paid you. That ties to bookkeeping in 9.8.

Tax handling ties back to SR.1. Enter your Section D taxes, run a direct booking test, and look at the tax line.

And migration effort. Time how long setup takes, and ask how you'd disconnect cleanly. Airbnb has a help article on switching software. Read it before you plan a move.

slides.title: A pricing tool needs a floor tied to your break-even, and a change log you read
rows: Set a nightly floor using your break-even math; confirm no date goes below it
Create a 1-night gap; see what the tool does
Set an override; wait two syncs; check it held
Check comps against Sam's 4.3 AirDNA work or PA.4 comps
Open the change log after three days: old rate, new rate, reason
Compare the rate on each channel for five dates (T3)
Price a 7-night stay on each channel; look for double discounts

box.label: Alder Street break-even
box.text: Break-even is a rate plus an occupancy. At Alder Street: 49.9% at a $205 average, or 57.1% at $180. Pick a floor that keeps your average above break-even.

slides.notes:
A pricing tool changes your rates every day. You need to know what it did and why, and you need limits it can't cross.

Airbnb has a built-in option called Smart Pricing, which adjusts prices by demand, on Airbnb only. A third-party tool, and PriceLabs from Sam's 9.13 is one example, usually sends rates to several channels through the PMS.

The first row is the one I'd test hardest. Break-even is a pair: an average rate and the occupancy you need at it. For Alder Street, that's 49.9% at a $205 average, or 57.1% at $180. The floor is a nightly minimum, not your average. Set it so a few low nights can't drag your average below break-even. So the floor comes from your numbers, not the tool's default.

Then read the change log after three days. Old rate, new rate, date, and reason. If you can't explain a change, you can't manage it. And price a 7-night stay on each channel to catch discounts stacking on top of each other.

slides.title: Score AI messaging on emergencies and escalation as hard as calendar sync
slides.keyline: It can answer questions, and it can't make promises.
rows: Ask about a detail only in an outdated document; it shouldn't use it
Ask an ambiguous question (T8); it holds or sends a holding reply
Ask for a discount; it must not promise one
Send "the CO alarm is beeping" (T9); time the human alert
Get the vendor's written data policy; see [Airbnb API terms](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3418)
Export the log: AI or human, sources used, approver, time
Test at night; review sent messages for off-platform payment requests
slides.notes:
AI messaging tools draft or send replies from your listing, house manual, and reservation data. They save time on routine questions. They also bring new risks: a wrong answer sent with confidence, a missed emergency, or guest data read by a system you didn't check.

So I hold them to one plain rule. It can answer questions, and it can't make promises. Refunds, discounts, early check-in exceptions, and damage claims go to a human.

The emergency test is the one I care about most. Words like fire, smoke, gas, carbon monoxide, flood, injury, or police should alert a named person at once. The guest should be told to leave and call 911 first. Send the test message and time the alert.

Also ask what guest data the tool reads and keeps, and whether it trains on your data. Get that in writing. Ask the vendor to confirm it follows Airbnb's API Terms of Service.

slides.title: Score is the sum of weight times rating, divided by the sum of weights
slides.text: **Weights (1 to 5):** how much a criterion counts. 5 means the operation fails without it. **Formula:** Score = sum(weight × rating) / sum(weights), from 1.00 to 5.00. **Example:** weights 5 and 1, rated 4 and 2: (5 × 4 + 1 × 2) / (5 + 1) = 22 / 6 = 3.67.
rows: Worked with a minor setting change
Works, but needs a manual step every time
Works only with a second tool or vendor support
slides.notes:
Scoring happens after the trial, never before. Each candidate is a whole stack: the PMS plus the pricing and messaging you'd run with it.

There are two numbers per criterion. The weight says how much it matters, from 1 to 5. You set weights on day one. The rating says how the tool did in your trial. A 5 worked with no workaround. A 1 failed or wasn't there.

Two rows need their own scale. Cost fit: 5 is well under budget, 3 is at budget, 1 is over. Setup effort: 5 is the easiest, 1 still wasn't working on day 14. Higher always means better.

Multiply each rating by its weight, add those up, and divide by the total of the weights. Say two criteria weigh 5 and 1, rated 4 and 2. That's 20 plus 2, which is 22, divided by 6, or 3.67. In a spreadsheet it's one SUMPRODUCT divided by a SUM.

slides.title: Knockouts come first, and a lead under 0.30 sends you to the top-weighted criteria

gates.q: Is a tool rated below 3 on any must-have?
gates.sub: Must-haves come from your operator profile
gates.no: Yes: that tool is out, whatever its score
Yes: no pick yet. Keep your setup or trial a new tool

gates.q: Are the top two rounded scores less than 0.30 apart?
gates.sub: Use scores rounded to two decimals. 0.30 is a teaching default (assumption)
gates.no: Yes: close call. The score doesn't decide

slides.notes:
Four rules turn scores into a decision. Apply them in order.

Rule 1 is the knockout. If a tool rates below 3 on anything you marked must-have, it's out. A great score can't make up for failing the one thing you can't live without.

Rule 2: if everyone gets knocked out, you haven't found your tool yet. Keep what you have, or trial another candidate.

Rule 3: compare the scores rounded to two decimals, the way the tables show them. If the top score leads by 0.30 or more, pick it. The 0.30 line is a teaching default, an assumption, not a law.

Rule 4 is the close call. If the gap is under 0.30, look only at the criteria with your top weight, usually 5. Count which tool rates higher on each. Ties count for neither. More wins picks it. If the count is equal, pick the tool rated higher on setup effort.

Every pick still waits on the price and terms in the next section.
slides.end: **Then pick.** A lead of 0.30 or more picks the leader. In a close call, count wins on your top-weight criteria only; equal ratings count for neither. More wins picks it, and an equal count goes to the tool rated higher on setup effort. Confirm price and terms in SR.5.7.

slides.title: Leave every vendor price blank until you copy it from a dated quote or page
rows: Base monthly price for your property count
Price lock, increases, data export on cancellation
slides.notes:
This part of the sheet is blank on purpose. Vendor pricing changes, and it often depends on property count and add-ons. Vrbo's integration article notes that software providers set their own pricing and billing models. So I don't put a single price on this template.

Fill each row from the vendor's own pricing page or a written quote, and date it. Base price for your property count. Per-booking or percentage fees. Payment-processing fees, if you become the merchant of record. Any add-ons you need for pricing, messaging, or a direct site. Setup fees, contract term, how much notice to cancel, whether the price is locked, and whether you can export your data when you leave.

The all-in monthly cost is base plus add-ons plus the per-booking fees you expect. Compare it to the budget in your profile. Fill this table in before you rate cost fit.

Recheck this table within 30 days of signing. If you share the comparison with anyone, recheck the terms first.

slides.title: Run a two-week trial on one real listing, with weights set on day 1
rows: Write the profile; set weights and must-haves. Export current reservations, rates, messages
Connect the PMS; choose the Airbnb sync mode on purpose. Enter SR.1 taxes and the permit number
Run T1 to T4. Connect pricing: floor, ceiling, minimum stays, one event override. Rerun T3
Load approved templates and the house manual. Run T8 to T10
Check the pricing log for dates below the floor. Run T5 and T6
Set up cleaner and co-host logins. Run T7
Export and reconcile a week. Send and chase vendor questions. Score and recommend

box.label: One PMS per listing
box.text: Never connect two PMSs to the same listing at once. Trial them one after the other, or on two similar listings.

slides.notes:
The trial runs two weeks on one real listing, on dates you can watch. Keep a log with the date, the test, the result, and a screenshot.

Day 1 is the one people rush. Write the profile and set weights and must-haves before you open any tool. Then save a full export of your current reservations, rates, and messages from each channel, so you can go back.

On day 2, connect the PMS and choose the Airbnb sync mode on purpose. Write down which one and why. Enter the taxes from SR.1 Section D and the permit number.

The middle days run the tests. They bring in the pricing tool and the messaging layer one at a time, so you can tell which piece caused a problem.

The last few days are exports, reconciling a week of bookings to payouts, and written questions to the vendor. Then you score.

You can't force a real booking or a guest change. If none arrives, mark that test not tested, and don't rate it above 3.

If you're trialing two tools, never connect both to the same listing at once.

slides.caption: Only run a real reservation through a platform if its terms allow it. Never use a test booking to create a review.
slides.notes:
These are the tests from the trial, and each one checks a handoff in the flow.

T1 through T4 are the calendar and rate tests. Block and unblock three nights. Change rates on five dates. Change a minimum stay. Every channel should match the PMS within the timing Vrbo and the vendor give you. Vrbo cites a few hours for availability.

T5 to T7 follow real bookings. Watch the first reservation on each channel. Don't create one. If you take direct bookings, run one on your own card and refund it, and check the tax matches SR.1 Section D.

T8 to T10 test the messaging layer. An ambiguous question about a small dog should get a hold or a holding reply, not a made-up yes. The carbon monoxide message should tell the guest to leave and call 911 first, and alert a real person. A discount request goes to a human.

Most of this carries no guest risk. Ask the platform before you run any real reservation through it.

slides.title: At Alder Street, Tool X scores 3.86 and Tool Y 3.66, a 0.20 gap that is a close call
slides.text: Profile: 1 leased apartment on Airbnb and Vrbo, a student plus a cleaner, $90 / month budget. Must-haves: channel connections and calendar sync. Weighted = weight × rating.
slides.notes:
Here's the worked example. Tool X and Tool Y are hypothetical. Tool X is a lighter channel manager with basic pricing links and messaging, quick to set up. Tool Y is a fuller PMS with a direct-booking site, owner statements, and more setup work. Every weight and rating here is an assumption for teaching.

Alder Street is one leased apartment on Airbnb and Vrbo, run by the student and a cleaner, with a $90 a month software budget. Cost and setup effort matter most. Direct booking barely matters, so it gets a weight of 1.

Read across. Tool Y rates higher on channel connections, pricing, messaging, and statements. Tool X wins big on setup and on cost fit, and those carry weights of 4 and 5.

The weights add to 29. Tool X totals 112, for a score of 3.86. Tool Y totals 106, for 3.66. That's a 0.20 gap. Now we go to the rules.

slides.title: A 1-1 count on the weight-5 rows hands Alder Street to Tool X on setup effort

nodes.d: Both rate 4+ on channel connections and calendar sync
Under the 0.30 line, so a close call
Y wins channels, X wins cost fit, sync ties. One win each
Equal count, so setup decides: X rates 5, Y rates 2
If its all-in price fits the $90 budget

slides.notes:
Now step through the rules for Alder Street.

Knockout first. The must-haves are channel connections and calendar sync. Both tools rate 4 or higher on both, so both pass. Nobody is knocked out, so Rule 2 doesn't apply.

Rule 3 is the margin. 3.86 minus 3.66 is 0.20. That's under the 0.30 line, so the score doesn't decide. It's a close call.

Rule 4 says count wins on the top-weight criteria only. Three carry a weight of 5: channel connections, calendar sync, and cost fit. Tool Y wins channel connections, 5 to 4. Tool X wins cost fit, 5 to 2. Sync is a tie, so it counts for neither. That's one win each.

On an equal count, the tool rated higher on setup and migration effort wins. Tool X rates 5 and Tool Y rates 2.

So Alder Street gets Tool X, on one condition. Its cost-fit 5 used the published price. Confirm that price in writing, and check it fits the $90 budget.

slides.title: At Cedar Ridge, Tool X is knocked out on direct booking before the scores matter
slides.text: Profile: 1 owned house, direct booking within 12 months, $100 / month budget. Must-haves: channel connections, calendar sync, and direct booking and payments.
slides.notes:
Same two tools, different operation. Cedar Ridge is one owned house. Maya and Chris run it with a cleaner and an on-call handyman, and they plan a direct-booking site within 12 months. Their budget is $100 a month, which is $1,200 a year.

Look at what changed in the weights. Direct booking goes from 1 to 5. Owner statements go from 2 to 4, because they need clean statements for their CPA. Setup effort and cost drop to 3.

Their must-haves add direct booking and payments. Tool X rates 2 there. Under Rule 1, Tool X is out before we even look at the scores.

The scores agree anyway. Weights add to 31. Tool X totals 105, for 3.39. Tool Y totals 125, for 4.03. Tool Y leads by 0.64, well past the 0.30 line.

slides.title: Even with direct booking weighted 1, Tool Y leads Cedar Ridge by exactly 0.30
slides.side:
A fair question: should direct booking count now if the site is a year away? Even then, Tool Y clears the 0.30 line, but only just.

The table misses one cost. Starting on Tool X means a second setup and a [migration](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2958) in a year, while the house is booked.

side_box.label: Condition
side_box.text: Confirm Tool Y's all-in price in SR.5.7. If it runs above $100 a month, Maya and Chris decide whether to accept that.

slides.notes:
Here's a fair challenge to that result. The direct site is a year away. Should direct booking really count now?

So rerun it with that weight cut from 5 to 1, and drop it as a must-have. The weights go from 31 to 27. Tool X loses 10 and gains 2, so 105 becomes 97. That's 97 over 27, or 3.59. Tool Y loses 25 and gains 5, so 125 becomes 105. That's 105 over 27, or 3.89. Tool Y leads by 0.30, exactly on the Rule 3 line. It still wins, but only just.

There's also a cost the table doesn't show. Starting on Tool X means a second setup and a migration next year while the house is taking bookings. Airbnb has a separate help article on switching software. Read it before you plan a move.

So Cedar Ridge gets Tool Y, once its all-in price is confirmed. Same tools, different answers, because the weights differ. That's why you set weights on day 1.

slides.title: The recommendation names the stack, the rule applied, and what would change it
rows: Who remits lodging tax by channel
Airbnb sync mode chosen and why
90 days after go-live (assumption), or when properties or channels change
slides.notes:
The last page of the template is the recommendation. It's one table, and it's the page you'll look back at later.

Name the stack: which PMS, which pricing tool, which messaging layer. Write the score, the margin, and which decision rule picked the winner. Note any knockouts, so you remember why a cheaper tool was ruled out.

Then the facts that follow from the choice. The all-in monthly cost with the date you checked it. Who is merchant of record on each channel. Who remits lodging tax on each channel. Which Airbnb sync mode you chose, and why.

The last rows keep it honest. What did you ask the vendor that's still open? What would change this decision? And when do you review it? I use 90 days after go-live as a teaching default, or sooner if your property count or channels change.

slides.title: Vendors confirm terms in writing, and your CPA confirms the tax reports
rows: Pricing, contract term, merchant-of-record setup per channel, data export, guest-data policy
The PMS separates platform-remitted tax from tax you owe; statements match your return
Which taxes you remit on direct bookings and wherever you become merchant of record
Sync mode and editing rules for your connected listings, before go-live
Whether any guest-screening or messaging rule in your policy affects setup
slides.caption: Bring these to each person below: the recommendation page, the SR.5.7 terms table, and the trial log.
slides.notes:
When you hand this off, bring the recommendation page, the pricing and terms table, and your trial log. Each person confirms a different piece.

Each vendor confirms in writing: current pricing, the contract term, the merchant-of-record setup for each channel, your rights to export data, and the guest-data policy. A sales call isn't enough. Get the email.

Your CPA confirms that the PMS reports keep platform-remitted tax separate from the tax you owe. They also confirm the owner statements give them what your return needs.

The tax agencies from SR.1 Section D confirm which taxes you remit on direct bookings, and anywhere the software makes you the merchant of record.

Airbnb and Vrbo, through their help centers or partner support, confirm the sync mode and editing rules before you go live.

And ask your insurer whether any guest-screening or messaging requirement in your policy changes how you set up the messaging tool.

slides.title: Most bad tool choices come from weights set late and tests that skip the handoffs
items: Setting weights after seeing the tools, so the favorite wins by design
Scoring from the feature list instead of the trial
Testing the screens, not the handoffs between PMS, pricing, and channels
Setting a pricing floor without your break-even math
Letting the AI promise refunds, discounts, or exceptions
Changing merchant of record without updating SR.1 Section D tax routing
slides.notes:
Six mistakes to watch for, and every one of them is on this sheet.

The first is the quiet one. If you set weights after you've seen the tools, you'll set them so your favorite wins. Set them on day 1.

Second, scoring from the feature list. Ratings come from what happened in your trial. Third, testing the screens and skipping the handoffs. The failures sit between the pieces.

Fourth, a pricing floor that isn't tied to your break-even. For Alder Street, that's the 49.9% and 57.1% math we looked at.

Fifth, letting the AI make promises. It answers questions. People handle refunds, discounts, and exceptions.

The last one is where this sheet meets SR.1. Does your recommendation change who's merchant of record on any channel? Then update SR.1 Section D tax routing before your first booking.

slides.notes:
These are the platform pages behind the rules on the slides. The full list, with how each one was checked, is in the SR.5 sources section.

Most were checked on September 25, 2026, through official-domain search. The switching-software and Smart Pricing articles were only seen in search results, so read those two yourself. Help centers change often, and sync options and payment rules are the kind of thing that gets updated. Open each page yourself before you go live, and put your own date next to it.
